extracted.intended_audience: Principal investigators and research teams preparing NIH/NIAID research plan sections (especially R01 applicants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting the Specific Aims and Research Strategy (Significance, Innovation, Approach, Preliminary Studies/Progress Report) for NIH R01 (and similar) grant applications, including formatting, organization, and reviewer-focused content. Emphasizes how to present aims, experimental plans, and supporting evidence to peer reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific Aims — one-page focused objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific Aims — a one-page statement of your objectives for the project. List two to three concrete objectives (aims) that are narrowly focused and achievable during the grant period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use at least half the page for a rationale and significance sentence starting with project goals; state hypothesis; describe how aims build on preliminary data; use strong verbs (identify, define, quantify, establish, determine); describe each aim in 1–3 sentences; consider bullets under each aim; use bolding/headers so reviewers can spot aims; keep to one page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research Strategy structure (Significance, Innovation, Approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Research Strategy comprises three main sections: Significance, Innovation, and Approach (plus Preliminary Studies or Progress Report for new vs renewal applications). Start each section with the appropriate header.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the Approach around the Specific Aims; you may integrate Preliminary Studies into any section but mark them clearly; for an R01 the Research Strategy (three main sections and preliminary studies) is limited to 12 pages. Use bold headers or consistent outlining/numbering throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and page limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow NIH formatting rules for font, page limits and other attachment rules; Research Strategy limited to 12 pages for R01s and Specific Aims to one page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write in a word processor, convert to PDF, and upload. Do not evade page limits by moving Research Plan content into other sections. Read the SF 424 Application Guide and Format Attachments instructions to ensure compliance; NIH may return applications that don't meet requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title — succinct, specific, within 200 characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the 200-character limit, include important information to distinguish your project, your goals, and the research problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the title succinct and specific (e.g., more than 'lymphocyte trafficking'); reflect goals, problem, and possibly approach; include appropriate keywords; use a different title for each application unless exceptions apply; a preliminary title helps focus writing but may change later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance — detailed context and importance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Significance section should give the most details about why the project matters, including the state of the field, knowledge gaps, and relevance to human disease and NIAID mission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide context: (1) state of field, (2) long-term research plans, (3) preliminary data. Explain how the project fills gaps and will advance the field; provide more basic biology if reviewers may be outside your subfield; use formatting and whitespace to highlight key points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Innovation — show how work is new and appropriate risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that the proposed research is new and unique (new avenues, novel hypothesis, new knowledge), but be cautious if you are a new investigator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New investigators should generally show refinement or new applications of existing concepts rather than radical paradigm shifts; if claiming a paradigm shift, present very strong supporting data and evidence of ability to do the work. Tie innovation to feasibility and supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach — experiments per aim with alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline a few sets of experiments to address each Specific Aim, including experimental details sufficient to convince reviewers you can carry out the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under each aim, describe initial experiments and branching next steps (if result X, follow pathway X; if Y, follow Y); include alternative experiments/contingency plans; cite publications showing capability; give more detail for methods you or your team have not previously used; omit extraneous information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor and Reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: For most applications, describe experimental design and methods and how they will achieve robust and unbiased results (Rigor and Reproducibility requirement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly address design elements that ensure robustness and lack of bias; this applies to research grants, career development, fellowship, and training applications. Include methods, controls, sample sizes, randomization/blinding if relevant, and analytic plans as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary Studies or Progress Report — demonstrate capability
rubrics_metrics.description: For new applications include preliminary studies showing you can handle the methods; for renewals include a Progress Report summarizing progress toward Specific Aims and key results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on your own lab's unpublished and published data where possible; give alternative interpretations of preliminary data to show critical thinking; clearly distinguish which data are yours vs others'; for progress reports include project period dates and account of published/unpublished results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipate reviewer questions and address them
rubrics_metrics.description: Proactively answer common reviewer concerns such as feasibility, over-ambitious scope, potential pitfalls and alternatives, whether experiments will yield meaningful data, and whether others are already doing the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend time thinking about issues specific to your research and address them in the Research Strategy; explicitly state contingency plans and how negative/surprising results will be handled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graphics and visual aids
rubrics_metrics.description: Use schematics, tables, illustrations, graphs, timetables, flowcharts, and decision trees to illustrate complex information and experimental plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Graphics can convey complex plans succinctly and add visual interest; include timetables/flowcharts to illustrate experimental decision trees; ensure graphics are readable and enhance reviewer understanding. For video, include evocative stills and a text summary that makes sense without the video; caption narration and follow SF 424 technical requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract/Project Summary and Project Narrative — clear, lay-accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a succinct Project Summary/Abstract and Project Narrative accessible to both scientists and lay audiences; both are used for assignment and public reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State significance to the field and NIAID mission, hypothesis, innovation, Specific Aims, and long-term objectives; write in lay language where possible; omit confidential/proprietary information; do not include graphs/images in the narrative; include appropriate, distinct keywords to aid referral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referencing publications — thorough but not excessive
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite all relevant publications underlying your concepts and methods; references demonstrate breadth of knowledge of the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite key and potential reviewer papers; include fewer than 100 citations if possible; list references in the Bibliography and References Cited form; add references for methods you do not describe in detail; you may reference unpublished work and personal communications where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization and readability — headers and consistent structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Present a well-organized, visually appealing, and readable Research Plan that reviewers can readily grasp.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bold headers, consistent outlining or numbering, whitespace and sectioning to highlight key points. Begin Research Strategy sections with Significance, Innovation, and Approach headers. Keep secondary sections clearly marked. If writing is not your strength, seek help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis and repetition — highlight key points
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeat and emphasize critical points so reviewers do not miss them; use bold or bold italics for emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeat key sentences or points and use formatting to draw attention. Also weave important points (e.g., significance, preliminary data, expertise) across sections rather than confining them to a single place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of experimental detail — tailored to experience
rubrics_metrics.description: Include enough experimental detail to convince reviewers you understand and can perform the methods; new investigators may need more detail than experienced ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite publications where you have demonstrated capability; provide more procedural detail for methods without a proven record; if space is limited, focus on experiments that highlight expertise and interest; list but do not overdescribe pedestrian or contracted methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omit extraneous information; stay within scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Trim the fat—omit information not needed to make your case. Do not pad other application sections with Research Plan content to evade page limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Including unnecessary detail gives reviewers ammunition to find flaws. Keep the Research Strategy focused; move administrative or unrelated material to appropriate sections and obey page limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track personnel, resources, timing, and budget during planning
rubrics_metrics.description: As you design experiments, keep a running tab of who will do the work, what equipment/supplies are needed, and how long steps take to inform the budget and timeline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these notes to create the Budget and Key Personnel sections later. New investigators should design a modest budget (rough guideline: under $250,000 for NIH modular budget). Include a timeline showing when aims will be completed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination across application components
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure consistency among Specific Aims, Research Strategy, biosketches, budget, and other application parts as plans evolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write iteratively: as experiments and plans change, update other sections to reflect who, what, when, where, and how much. Program staff may return non-responsive applications; confirm that your application meets the NOFO or PA's objectives and requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sample applications to calibrate strategy and detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult NIH sample applications to see diverse successful strategies and the level of detail used by other PIs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review sample Significance and Approach sections to learn how experienced and new investigators presented their plans; emulate structures and tactics that fit your situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Big Three reviewer questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers will look for three basic things: whether the research can move the field forward; whether the field is important to human health; and whether the applicant team can carry out the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make these points explicit across the application: demonstrate impact on the field/health, clarify importance to human health, and provide evidence (preliminary data, biosketches, resources) that you and your team can execute the project.
